annotation.reasoning_summary: Polygon features represent housing association property footprints/blocks, i.e. discrete real-world objects. They do not form a tessellation or reporting-unit coverage, so geometry is PlainVectorRegion and entity is ObjectDS.
Point geometry with each feature representing a distinct archaeological find/cesspit at an address; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point geometry with each feature representing a named archaeological find/location (object code, location, caption, photos); classify as ObjectDS rather than amount or event.
Polygons map archaeological sites/vindplaatsen as discrete identified places, not a tessellation or reporting unit. The decisive rule is ObjectDS for bounded real-world sites/features.
Polygons mark selected BBQ restriction/applicability areas around parks, not a full tessellation or reporting units; this fits a bounded patch/zone with policy restrictions.

Polygon areas are selected conservation zones, not a complete tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS: protected city/district heritage areas are bounded applicability zones where the protection applies.

Point geometry with each feature representing a wild bee observation site (area/year list of observed bee species), so this is an object/observation-location layer rather than an amount or event layer.
Point geometry with 111 features; each point represents a honey bee site/apiary object, with colony/hive counts as attributes rather than the main phenomenon.

Polygons form a near-area-wide zoning/soil-quality partition with zone and sanering classifications, so geometry is tessellation and the main meaning is selected applicability/phenomenon areas rather than objects or reporting units.
Point geometry with 70k individual tree records; each point represents a distinct tree object with species, year, owner, and manager attributes, not a measurement or event layer.

Point geometry with 70k mapped tree features; the layer represents identifiable real-world objects (trees), not measurements or events. Numeric fields are attributes of the trees, not the main phenomenon.
Point features are individual trees, and the attributes identify each tree as a distinct mapped object rather than a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual trees (named species/IDs, planting year, owner/manager, height), so this is a point object layer rather than measurements or events.
Point features map individual compost locations/facilities named by street and initiative details, so the decisive rule is point objects rather than amounts or events.

Polygons are named camera areas tied to overlast enforcement, so they represent selected affected zones rather than objects; the region layer is a tessellated set of area patches, not a full reporting-unit lattice.
Point geometry with each feature representing a distinct tree object (Canadian poplars) identified by tree number and species; the measures/planning fields are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Point features represent individual crowd-monitoring sensors/cameras; the decisive rule is points as distinct real-world objects, not measurements or events.

Polygon areas are selected cultural-historical exploration zones, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS: these are bounded areas where a phenomenon/assessment applies, rather than discrete mapped objects or coverage classes.
Point layer of knotweed occurrences; each point represents a mapped infestation/object location, not a measurement or event. Numeric area fields are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Points represent ecopassage problem locations/structures and related mitigation objects (e.g., bridges, passages, underpasses), so PointDS with ObjectDS is the best fit.

Polygon regions are selected potential wind-energy areas, not a full tessellation or reporting units; the decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded phenomenon areas. Numeric MW/GWh are attributes of these areas, not the main mapped phenomenon.

Point features represent individual stemlocaties/stemdistrict polling locations for the 2019 European Parliament election; the mapped thing is the voting location, not a measured field or event. Numeric vote fields are attributes, so ObjectDS, and the geometry is PointDS.
Point layer of individual trees/nest locations; the mapped thing is a distinct real-world object (tree/record), not a measurement or event.
Polygon areas represent pedicab allowed/forbidden zones and restrictions, not a tessellated reporting unit. The decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded applicability/restriction areas.
Point geometry with categorical labels for pedicab and carriage stand locations; the mapped thing is the stand/pitch itself, so this is an object layer.
Point geometry and the layer maps distinct non-residential facilities/addresses (e.g., church, office, restaurant); the numeric fields are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Polygon layer classifies each area by function mix (wonen/voorzieningen/werken) with categorical CAT labels, so it is a full-area thematic coverage rather than reporting units or discrete objects.

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so geometry is VectorTessellation. The layer is a reporting-unit geography (buurtcombinaties/wijken/stadsdeel codes), which makes it LatticeDS rather than object or patch.
Neighborhoods are reporting/statistical units that partition the city area, so geometry is VectorTessellation and entity is LatticeDS.

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so Geometry is VectorTessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting-unit keywords (buurt/buurten/stadsdeel), which makes this a lattice of statistical neighborhoods rather than objects or patches.

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so geometry is VectorTessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units: buurt/buurten and stadsdeel are administrative neighborhood units, so LatticeDS.
City districts are administrative/reporting units that partition the city area, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entity is LatticeDS.
City districts are reporting/administrative units that partition the city area, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entity is LatticeDS.

The layer is a set of named Amsterdam areas that function as reporting/administrative units (e.g., Gebied, Stadsdeel_code), so the decisive rule is reporting units -> LatticeDS. The polygons also form a near-complete area division, so geometry is VectorTessellation.
The layer is a partition of Amsterdam into named gebieden/areas, with area codes and reported area sizes, so it fits a reporting-unit tessellation (LatticeDS) rather than a patch or object.

Polygons are practice areas that partition the city into reporting/administrative-style units; the decisive rule is reporting units, so ENTITY = LatticeDS. Geometry is VectorTessellation because the regions form a near-complete areal partition.

The layer is a set of named practice areas that partition Amsterdam into area units, so it fits VectorTessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units, supported by district-like area names and Stadsdeel_code, so LatticeDS.
The layer is noise contours for industry; polygons represent contour bands/interval zones, not a full tessellation or objects. Decisive rule: contour/interval region layer.
Polygon regions represent noise contour bands (55-60, 60-65 dB, etc.), so the decisive rule is contour/interval zones rather than objects or reporting units.
Polygon areas represent noise contour bands (e.g., 50–55 dB, >70 dB), so this is a contour/interval zone layer rather than objects or reporting units.
Polygon layer of noise contour bands (50-55 dB, etc.); this is an isoline/interval-class map rather than objects or reporting units.

Point geometries mark individual voting locations/stembureaus. The layer is about polling station places with election results as attributes, so the decisive rule is point objects rather than amounts or events.
Point geometry; each point is a distinct green-roof site/place (addressed object) with attributes like type, year, and area, so ObjectDS rather than AmountDS.

Land use is a full-area thematic classification, so the polygons represent exhaustive coverage of the study area; the polygon layer is a tessellation and the decisive rule is CoverageDS before ObjectDS/PatchDS.
Point geometry with named historical buildings/structures as the mapped features, so this is ObjectDS; the dates are attributes, not the main phenomenon.

Polygon features are discrete municipalities/areas rather than a full tessellation, and the layer name/metadata suggest the mapped thing is the area itself ('How big is Amsterdam'), so ObjectDS is the best fit.
Polygon features describe dog off-leash and ban zones; this is a selected restriction/phenomenon area, not a reporting unit or full tessellation. PatchDS fits the area-where-rules-apply meaning.
Polygon features represent named green-structure sites/places like parks, cemeteries, sports parks, and gardens; these are mapped as discrete objects rather than a tessellation or reporting units.
Point features map individual elm trees as identifiable real-world objects; numeric fields are just attributes, so the decisive rule is ObjectDS for discrete assets.

Point geometry with 128 mapped housing sites; each point represents a discrete youth/student housing project or facility, not a measurement or event. The numeric woning count is an attribute, while the mapped feature is the object.
Point layer of individual chestnut trees; the mapped things are distinct objects, and the Aantasting field is just an attribute of each tree.
Point geometries sample groundwater/drought-related measurements (Maaiveld, GLG, GLG_maaiveld); the layer is a point-measurement dataset rather than objects or areas.
Polygon regions map flood risk/extent categories with probability and depth classes; this is a selected phenomenon zone, not a reporting unit or full tessellation, so PatchDS with PlainVectorRegion.
Point geometry with 45 market locations; the layer maps identifiable markets as places/facilities, not measurements or events.
Point geometries, and each point represents a named green monument/object (parks, gardens, bridges, monuments) rather than a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual monumental trees, i.e., discrete real-world objects; the decisive rule is points-to-objects, not amounts or events.
Point geometries map discrete monuments/buildings as named heritage objects; the decisive rule is PointDS + ObjectDS, not AmountDS because numeric fields are identifiers/attributes.
Point geometry with each point marking a specific quay-wall plant occurrence/object at a named location. The main mapped phenomenon is the mapped plant occurrence, not an amount or event.

Polygon layer forms a near-complete tessellation of Amsterdam subareas, and the main phenomenon is numeric NO2 values over time (concentration/average measurements), so this is a tessellated amount map.
Point geometry with NO2 measurement locations; the decisive rule is PointMeasuresDS because points sample a continuous environmental phenomenon at locations.

Polygon regions do not form a full tessellation, so geometry is PlainVectorRegion. The layer name ‘Oergeul/Primeval gulch’ suggests selected phenomenon areas rather than discrete objects, so PatchDS fits the patch/area-of-application rule.
Point features represent individual sounding/borehole observations with project IDs and measurement attributes; this is a point object dataset, not a point-measurement layer.
Development neighbourhoods are reporting/statistical areas in Amsterdam, and the polygons form a near-complete set of buurt units; this follows the reporting-unit/tessellation rule.
Point geometry with 206 features; the layer maps public toilets as distinct facilities/objects, not measurements or events.

Polygon features are neighbourhoods/buurt areas, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entity is a reporting-unit layer (LatticeDS). The policy text is attached to these units rather than mapping a full-area coverage or a single object.
Polygon zones for parking standards; not a tessellation or reporting unit. The layer maps bounded applicability areas for parking rules, so PatchDS best fits.
Polygons represent named parks and green spaces, i.e. discrete mapped objects; the layer is not a reporting-unit tessellation or full-area coverage. Numeric area is just an attribute, so ObjectDS.
Postcode/buurt polygons are reporting units that partition the area, so Geometry is VectorTessellation and Entity is LatticeDS; the numeric area field is just an attribute, not the main phenomenon.

Polygons are postcode/buurt reporting units that partition the city area, so VectorTessellation applies; the decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical unit -> LatticeDS, not AmountDS despite the area field.
Postcode6 and buurtcode are reporting/statistical units, and the polygons form a postcode-area tessellation; classify by the reporting-unit rule.
LineString features representing plus and main infrastructure networks (roads/transport links); the decisive rule is the route/system network branch, not the numeric attributes.

Polygon areas representing pedestrian plus-network zones, not a full tessellation. The decisive entity rule is PatchDS because these are selected bounded zones/areas of applicability rather than discrete objects or reporting units.
Point features with location names like bridges, sluices, and facilities indicate discrete mapped objects; the layer is not a measurement, event, or network, so ObjectDS fits best.

Geometry is PointDS because all features are points. Entity is ObjectDS because the points mark distinct privacy-related items/locations (research, risk analysis, investigations) rather than measurements, events, or amounts.
Point geometry with named locations/addresses for privacy car fleet scan sites; the points represent distinct monitoring locations/objects, not measurements or events.

Point geometry with 750 polling-location features; the layer maps distinct stemlocaties/Stemdistrict voting places, so ObjectDS fits better than AmountDS. The election counts are attributes of those point objects, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Polygons are selected rainproof drainage areas, not a full tessellation or reporting-unit map; the layer maps where high groundwater drainage is possible, so PatchDS fits best.

Polygon areas represent Rainproof hydro units tied to neighborhood solutions for stormwater overlast, so they are selected phenomenon zones rather than a full tessellation or reporting-unit lattice. PatchDS fits the bounded applicability/affected areas; geometry is PlainVectorRegion because the polygons do not form a complete partition.

Polygons represent rainproof bottleneck areas/urgent water problem zones rather than discrete objects; the layer is selected phenomenon areas, not a full coverage class or reporting-unit lattice. Reporting-unit terms appear in names, but the decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded affected zones.

Polygon features are discrete selected areas for Rainproof polder sewerage locations, not a full tessellation or reporting units; the layer is best read as bounded intervention zones/areas of applicability, so PatchDS.
Point geometry with 319 individual religious buildings/locations; the mapped phenomenon is identifiable places/facilities (religious sites), so ObjectDS.

Line geometry with sidewalk segments; the layer mainly maps sidewalk width and space-claim conditions along street segments, which are treated as applied zones/phenomenon extents rather than discrete objects or a transport network.
Line geometry with street/road segments for mopeds on the roadway; this is a connected transport route system, so NetworkDS is the decisive entity choice.
Point geometry with 818 public playground/sport facility locations; the mapped features are identifiable objects/places, not measurements or events.
Point features represent city farming locations/sites with names, addresses, and project/status attributes; this is a set of identifiable objects, not a measurement or event layer.
Polygons represent named city farming sites/parks with addresses and websites, so the mapped features are discrete objects; they are not a full tessellation or a patch/policy area.
Point features represent distinct city pilot initiatives/locations (initiative, activity, sector, year); this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Major streets are a connected street system, and the features are LineStrings; decisive rule is NetworkDS for route/street infrastructure.
LineString features and the title/attributes indicate a district heating/cooling transport system, so the decisive rule is network infrastructure.

Polygon layer of many neighbourhood zones for district heating/cooling; the areas are selected applicability/phenomenon zones rather than reporting units or full coverage, so VectorTessellation + PatchDS.

Polygon areas depict strategic housing development zones/areas of intervention, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded phenomenon/policy areas; geometry is PlainVectorRegion because the polygons do not form a complete partition.

Point features represent individual local farming products businesses/locations with names, addresses, products, and websites, so this is a point object layer rather than measures, events, or a network.
LineString features representing tram and metro lines; decisive rule is connected transport network infrastructure.
LineString features named tram and metro lines; the decisive rule is network infrastructure/route system, so Geometry is LineDS and Entity is NetworkDS.
Point features representing tram stops and metro stations; the mapped phenomenon is identifiable transit objects, not amounts or events.
Point geometries for tram stops and metro stations; each point is a distinct transit object/facility, not a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual traffic light locations/intersections, so the layer maps distinct objects rather than measurements, events, or areas.
Line geometries with road names/link IDs and traffic forecast counts by time/vehicle type; this is a line-based amount layer, not a generic network map.

Point features represent individual voting locations (stemlocaties) such as schools and buildings; the numeric vote fields are attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon. ObjectDS fits the mapped places, and PointDS follows the point geometry.
Point geometry with tree-specific identifiers and species/plant-year attributes; the mapped features are individual trees as discrete objects, not amounts or events.
Point geometry with 566 mapped traffic information system devices (cameras, displays, detectors, etc.); the layer is about identifiable installed objects, not measurements or network lines.
Point features represent individual traffic information system installations/controlled access points (BFA objects). The layer is about identifiable facilities/assets, not measurements or events.
Point geometry with each feature representing a breeding-bird observation/location tied to a street address or nesting place; not a measurement layer, so ObjectDS fits best.
Point geometries for individual benches; the mapped thing is the bench itself, so ObjectDS (not amount or event).
Line geometry with 9,617 street segments; the layer maps walkability conditions on individual street objects/segments, not a network flow or amount layer.
Point geometry with each point marking a specific wall-art work at an address; the layer is about identifiable art objects, not measurements or events.
Polygons represent welstandniveau zones/areas of applicability, not a full tessellation or reporting units, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS (policy/condition areas).

Polygons represent Amsterdam welstandssystemen: a full-area thematic classification of urban built environment zones, so geometry is plain regions and the entity is CoverageDS (area-wide categorical coverage).
Point geometries map WWII attack occurrences and damage incidents at addresses; the decisive rule is EventDS for something that happened at a location.

Polygons represent discrete housing plan project areas named by project/fase, not a full-area coverage or reporting lattice; numeric dwelling counts are attributes, so the decisive rule is object polygons with tessellated housing project areas.
Point features mark individual self-build plot projects/sites with names and attributes; this is a set of discrete objects, not a measurement or network.
Polygon features classify areas by heritage/solar-panel category ('Categorie' with Attentie, Historisch ruim, etc.), indicating a full-area thematic coverage rather than objects or reporting units.

Point features represent solar-panel locations, and the mapped phenomenon is numeric magnitude (detected panels/power). Classified as PointDS with AmountDS rather than object or coverage because the layer emphasizes counts/capacity at points.
Point geometry with named swimming locations/facilities (baths, beaches, playgrounds) makes this a set of identifiable objects, not measurements or events.
